Hepatitis A.risk_groups: travelers to endemic regions, people with poor sanitation, drug users, men who have sex with men, close contacts of infected individuals
progression: ingestion of virus through contaminated sources
viral replication in liver
onset of symptoms and liver inflammation
recovery without chronic infection
Hepatitis A.duration: weeks to months (usually resolves within 6 months)
complications: liver failure (rare), prolonged symptoms, higher risk in older adults or those with liver disease
home_remedy: rest, hydration, healthy diet, avoid alcohol

Hepatitis A.when_to_see_doctor: jaundice, persistent vomiting, abdominal pain, suspected exposure
Hepatitis A.emergency_signs: confusion, severe vomiting, signs of liver failure, altered consciousness
prevention: hepatitis A vaccination, hand hygiene, safe food and water practices
Hepatitis A.contagious_period: about 2 weeks before symptoms to up to 3 weeks after symptom onset
Hepatitis A.special_notes: does not cause chronic liver disease, immunity develops after infection or vaccination, highly preventable

Hepatitis B.description: viral liver infection that can be acute or chronic, causing liver inflammation and potential long-term liver damage
Hepatitis B.cause: hepatitis B virus (HBV) infecting liver cells
Hepatitis B.transmission: contact with infected blood or body fluids, unprotected sexual contact, sharing needles, mother-to-child during childbirth
Hepatitis B.risk_groups: healthcare workers, people with multiple sexual partners, intravenous drug users, travelers to endemic regions, infants born to infected mothers
progression: exposure to infected blood or body fluids
viral replication in liver
acute infection with symptoms or asymptomatic phase
recovery or progression to chronic infection and liver damage
complications: chronic hepatitis, cirrhosis, liver failure, liver cancer, hepatitis D co-infection
home_remedy: rest, hydration, healthy diet, avoid alcohol
avoid: alcohol, sharing needles, unprotected sex, hepatotoxic substances
Hepatitis B.when_to_see_doctor: jaundice, persistent fatigue, abdominal pain, exposure risk
Hepatitis B.emergency_signs: severe abdominal pain, confusion, signs of liver failure, vomiting blood
prevention: hepatitis B vaccination, safe sex practices, sterile needle use, screening of blood products
Hepatitis B.contagious_period: while virus is present in blood and body fluids (can be lifelong in chronic cases)
Hepatitis B.special_notes: chronic infection risk higher in infants, antiviral therapy may be required, lifelong monitoring needed in chronic cases

Mumps.description: contagious viral infection affecting the salivary glands, leading to swelling, fever, and systemic symptoms
Mumps.transmission: respiratory droplets, direct contact with saliva, sharing contaminated items
Mumps.risk_groups: unvaccinated individuals, children, students in close-contact settings, healthcare workers, travelers to endemic areas

progression: exposure to virus via respiratory droplets or saliva
viral replication in upper respiratory tract
spread to salivary glands causing swelling
recovery or rare complications affecting other organs
Mumps.common_locations: salivary glands (parotid), respiratory tract, testes, ovaries, pancreas, brain
complications: meningitis, encephalitis, orchitis, oophoritis, pancreatitis, hearing loss, miscarriage
home_remedy: rest, hydration, pain relief, warm or cold compress on glands, soft diet
avoid: close contact with others, sharing utensils, public exposure during contagious period
Mumps.when_to_see_doctor: swelling of glands, high fever, severe headache, testicular pain, persistent symptoms
Mumps.emergency_signs: seizures, stiff neck, confusion, severe headache, drowsiness

Mumps.contagious_period: a few days before swelling until about 5 days after onset

Rubella.description: contagious viral infection characterized by mild fever and rash, but can cause severe birth defects if contracted during pregnancy
Rubella.transmission: airborne droplets from coughing or sneezing, direct contact, mother-to-fetus during pregnancy
Rubella.risk_groups: unvaccinated individuals, pregnant women, travelers to endemic regions, children
symptoms: rash starting on face and spreading to body
progression: exposure to virus via respiratory droplets
viral replication in respiratory tract
spread through bloodstream
development of rash and mild systemic symptoms
Rubella.common_locations: skin, lymph nodes, respiratory tract, fetus (in congenital infection)
complications: arthritis, encephalitis (rare), congenital rubella syndrome, miscarriage, birth defects
home_remedy: rest, hydration, fever management with acetaminophen
avoid: contact with pregnant women, skipping vaccination, crowded environments during infection
Rubella.when_to_see_doctor: rash with fever, exposure history, pregnancy exposure
prevention: MMR vaccination, isolation during infection, hygiene practices
Rubella.contagious_period: about 1 week before rash to 7 days after rash onset
Rubella.special_notes: often mild in children but dangerous in pregnancy, lifelong immunity after infection or vaccination, no specific antiviral treatment

Chickenpox.description: highly contagious viral infection causing itchy fluid-filled blisters, primarily affecting children but possible at any age

Chickenpox.transmission: airborne droplets, direct contact with blister fluid, contact with shingles lesions, highly infectious before rash appears
Chickenpox.risk_groups: unvaccinated individuals, children, pregnant women, newborns, adolescents, adults, immunocompromised individuals

itchy red rash progressing to fluid-filled blisters
blisters that scab over within about a week
rash starting on chest, back, face and spreading across body
up to hundreds of lesions in severe cases
progression: initial mild fever and fatigue
appearance of red spots on skin
formation of fluid-filled blisters
blisters crust over and heal within 1-2 weeks
Chickenpox.common_locations: face, chest, back, scalp, arms, legs, mouth
complications: bacterial skin infection, pneumonia, encephalitis, dehydration, fetal complications, severe disease in adults
home_remedy: rest, hydration, soothing lotions, oatmeal baths, antihistamines for itching
avoid: scratching, aspirin (risk of Reye syndrome), ibuprofen in some cases, close contact with others
Chickenpox.when_to_see_doctor: high fever, severe rash, breathing difficulty, immunocompromised status, pregnancy exposure
Chickenpox.emergency_signs: difficulty breathing, severe dehydration, neurological symptoms, persistent vomiting, altered consciousness
prevention: varicella vaccination (2 doses), avoiding contact with infected individuals, hygiene practices
Chickenpox.contagious_period: 1-2 days before rash until all lesions crust over

Rabies.description: fatal viral infection affecting the central nervous system leading to brain inflammation and death if untreated before symptom onset
Rabies.cause: rabies virus (a lyssavirus) transmitted through infected animal saliva
Rabies.transmission: bites or scratches from infected animals, saliva contact with open wounds or mucous membranes
Rabies.risk_groups: people exposed to wild animals, travelers to endemic regions, veterinarians, animal handlers, outdoor workers
Rabies.incubation_period: weeks to months (variable depending on exposure site)
symptoms: tingling or itching at bite site
progression: virus enters body through bite or scratch

causes brain inflammation and neurological symptoms
progression to coma and death if untreated
Rabies.common_locations: brain, central nervous system, salivary glands
Rabies.duration: days to weeks after symptom onset (rapid progression)
complications: encephalitis, paralysis, respiratory failure, death
home_remedy: none
avoid: contact with wild or unvaccinated animals, delayed post-exposure treatment
Rabies.when_to_see_doctor: any animal bite or suspected exposure, especially from wild animals
Rabies.emergency_signs: confusion, hallucinations, difficulty swallowing, paralysis, seizures
prevention: rabies vaccination (pre- and post-exposure), wound cleaning, avoiding animal contact, vaccinating pets
Rabies.contagious_period: present in saliva of infected animals, human-to-human transmission extremely rare
Rabies.special_notes: nearly 100% fatal after symptom onset, post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) is highly effective if given early, bats are a major source in some regions

Leprosy.description: chronic bacterial infection affecting skin, peripheral nerves, and mucous membranes leading to progressive damage and disability if untreated
Leprosy.cause: Mycobacterium leprae bacteria infecting skin and nerves
Leprosy.transmission: prolonged close contact via respiratory droplets or nasal secretions from untreated individuals
Leprosy.risk_groups: people in endemic regions, close contacts of infected individuals, children, immunocompromised individuals

numbness in hands, arms, feet, or legs
progression: infection via respiratory exposure
slow bacterial growth affecting skin and nerves
development of sensory loss and skin lesions
nerve damage and disability if untreated
Leprosy.common_locations: skin, peripheral nerves, face, hands, feet
Leprosy.duration: chronic, may last years without treatment
complications: nerve damage, loss of sensation, muscle weakness, deformities, disability
home_remedy: none
avoid: delayed treatment, close contact without precautions, neglect of symptoms
Leprosy.when_to_see_doctor: persistent skin lesions, numbness, weakness, contact with infected person
Leprosy.emergency_signs: severe nerve damage, loss of function, secondary infections
prevention: early diagnosis and treatment, avoiding prolonged close contact with untreated cases
Leprosy.contagious_period: low, mainly in untreated individuals (reduced after starting treatment)
Leprosy.special_notes: treatable with multi-drug therapy, early treatment prevents disability, stigma associated with disease despite low infectivity

Whooping Cough.description: highly contagious bacterial respiratory infection causing severe coughing fits and airway inflammation
Whooping Cough.cause: Bordetella pertussis bacteria damaging respiratory cilia and releasing toxins
Whooping Cough.transmission: airborne droplets from coughing or sneezing, close contact in shared airspace
Whooping Cough.risk_groups: infants under 1 year, unvaccinated individuals, elderly, people with asthma or weakened immune systems
symptoms: mild cough and runny nose (early stage)
whooping sound during inhalation after coughing
progression: initial mild cold-like symptoms (catarrhal stage)
progression to severe coughing fits (paroxysmal stage)
gradual recovery with reduced coughing (convalescent stage)
prolonged cough may persist for weeks
complications: pneumonia, apnea (in infants), seizures, brain damage, death (especially in infants)
home_remedy: rest, hydration, humidified air, supportive care
avoid: close contact with others, exposure of infants, delayed treatment
Whooping Cough.when_to_see_doctor: persistent severe cough, coughing fits, vomiting after coughing, infant symptoms
Whooping Cough.emergency_signs: difficulty breathing, apnea, bluish skin, seizures, severe exhaustion
prevention: vaccination (DTaP/Tdap), antibiotics after exposure, hygiene practices
Whooping Cough.contagious_period: from early symptoms up to 2 weeks after coughing begins (shorter with antibiotics)
Whooping Cough.special_notes: early antibiotic treatment reduces severity and spread, immunity not lifelong, infants are at highest risk

Tetanus.description: serious bacterial infection affecting the nervous system causing muscle stiffness and painful spasms
Tetanus.cause: Clostridium tetani bacteria producing a neurotoxin that affects motor nerves
Tetanus.transmission: contamination of wounds with bacterial spores from soil, dust, or animal waste (not person-to-person)
Tetanus.risk_groups: unvaccinated individuals, people with deep or contaminated wounds, intravenous drug users, newborns in unsanitary conditions

progression: spores enter body through wound
bacteria produce toxin in anaerobic conditions
toxin spreads via nerves to central nervous system
muscle rigidity and severe spasms develop
Tetanus.common_locations: nervous system, muscles, jaw, neck, back
Tetanus.duration: weeks to months (recovery may be prolonged)
complications: respiratory failure, fractures from spasms, pneumonia, autonomic instability, death
home_remedy: none
avoid: untreated wounds, poor hygiene, missing vaccinations
Tetanus.when_to_see_doctor: deep or contaminated wounds, unknown vaccination status, muscle stiffness or spasms
Tetanus.emergency_signs: difficulty breathing, severe spasms, inability to swallow, generalized rigidity
prevention: vaccination (DTaP/Tdap), booster doses every 10 years, proper wound care, sterile practices
Tetanus.special_notes: not spread person-to-person, neonatal tetanus occurs in unsanitary conditions, early vaccination is highly effective

Diphtheria.description: serious bacterial infection caused by toxin-producing bacteria leading to tissue damage, especially in the respiratory tract

toxin production causing tissue damage
systemic complications if untreated
complications: airway obstruction, myocarditis, nerve damage, respiratory failure, death
home_remedy: none
avoid: close contact with infected individuals, skipping vaccination, delayed treatment
Diphtheria.when_to_see_doctor: sore throat with membrane, breathing difficulty, exposure history
Diphtheria.emergency_signs: severe breathing difficulty, airway blockage, heart problems, neurological symptoms
prevention: vaccination (DTaP/Tdap), antibiotics for close contacts, hygiene practices
Diphtheria.contagious_period: until about 48 hours after starting antibiotics
Diphtheria.special_notes: toxin causes most damage rather than bacteria itself, early antitoxin treatment is critical, vaccination highly effective

Japanese Encephalitis.description: mosquito-borne viral infection causing inflammation of the brain, potentially leading to severe neurological damage or death
Japanese Encephalitis.transmission: bite of infected mosquitoes (mainly Culex species), not spread person-to-person
Japanese Encephalitis.risk_groups: people living in rural Asia, long-term travelers to endemic regions, outdoor workers, laboratory personnel
progression: infection via mosquito bite
viral replication in bloodstream
invasion of central nervous system
encephalitis with neurological symptoms
Japanese Encephalitis.duration: days to weeks (neurological recovery may take longer)
complications: brain damage, seizures, paralysis, coma, permanent disability, death
home_remedy: none
avoid: mosquito bites, travel without protection, staying in high-risk rural areas without precautions
Japanese Encephalitis.when_to_see_doctor: fever with neurological symptoms, travel history to endemic areas
Japanese Encephalitis.emergency_signs: seizures, coma, severe confusion, inability to wake
prevention: JE vaccination, mosquito control, insect repellents, protective clothing
Japanese Encephalitis.special_notes: most infections are asymptomatic, severe cases have high mortality, survivors may have long-term neurological deficits

Plague.description: severe bacterial infection transmitted from animals to humans, historically associated with epidemics and capable of causing rapid systemic illness

Plague.transmission: flea bites from infected rodents, contact with infected animal tissues or fluids, inhalation of infectious droplets (pneumonic form)

Plague.duration: days to weeks (rapid progression if untreated)
complications: sepsis, respiratory failure, organ failure, shock, death

avoid: flea exposure, contact with infected animals, handling animals without protection
Plague.when_to_see_doctor: fever with swollen lymph nodes, recent exposure to rodents or fleas, respiratory symptoms after exposure
Plague.emergency_signs: severe breathing difficulty, shock, confusion, bleeding, rapid deterioration
prevention: flea control, avoiding rodent exposure, protective equipment when handling animals, early antibiotic treatment
Plague.contagious_period: pneumonic plague can spread person-to-person via droplets
Plague.special_notes: requires urgent antibiotic treatment, pneumonic form is highly contagious, outbreaks linked to rodent populations and fleas

Zika Virus Infection.description: mosquito-borne viral infection usually causing mild illness but associated with serious complications during pregnancy and rare neurological disorders

Zika Virus Infection.emergency_signs: paralysis, severe neurological symptoms, confusion, difficulty breathing
prevention: mosquito control, insect repellents, protective clothing, safe sex practices
Zika Virus Infection.contagious_period: present in blood and bodily fluids for days to weeks (sexual transmission possible longer)
Zika Virus Infection.special_notes: often asymptomatic, major concern is during pregnancy, no vaccine or specific antiviral treatment available

Amoebiasis.contagious_period: while parasite cysts are shed in stool

Hand-Foot-Mouth Disease.description: common contagious viral infection primarily affecting children, characterized by sores in the mouth and rash on hands and feet

home_remedy: hydration, rest, pain relief (acetaminophen or ibuprofen), saltwater rinses

Hand-Foot-Mouth Disease.when_to_see_doctor: persistent fever, difficulty swallowing, dehydration signs, worsening symptoms

Hand-Foot-Mouth Disease.contagious_period: most contagious during first week, may spread for weeks via stool
Hand-Foot-Mouth Disease.special_notes: antibiotics ineffective, usually self-limiting, common in summer and early fall

Hantavirus Infection.description: rare but severe viral disease causing respiratory failure and systemic illness due to infection from rodent-borne viruses

Hantavirus Infection.special_notes: high fatality rate in severe cases, early recognition critical, more common in rural settings

Scrub Typhus.description: bacterial infection transmitted by mite larvae causing fever, rash, and systemic illness common in rural tropical regions
Scrub Typhus.cause: Orientia tsutsugamushi bacteria infecting endothelial cells
Scrub Typhus.transmission: bite of infected chiggers (larval mites), not spread person-to-person

Hypertension.description: chronic medical condition characterized by persistently elevated arterial blood pressure increasing risk of cardiovascular diseases

sustained elevation damages blood vessels
strain on heart and organs
development of complications over time

Hypertension.emergency_signs: hypertensive crisis (very high BP), chest pain, severe headache, confusion, vision changes
prevention: healthy diet, regular exercise, maintaining healthy weight, limiting alcohol, regular monitoring

Heart Attack.description: acute medical emergency caused by sudden blockage of blood flow to the heart muscle leading to tissue damage or death

progression: plaque rupture in coronary artery
formation of blood clot
blockage of blood flow to heart muscle
irreversible damage to heart tissue

home_remedy: none

Heart Attack.when_to_see_doctor: chest pain, shortness of breath, known heart disease symptoms

rapid cell death within minutes
neurological deficits or permanent damage

Stroke.special_notes: requires immediate emergency care, early treatment improves outcomes, TIA (mini-stroke) is a warning sign

Atherosclerosis.description: chronic condition characterized by buildup of fatty plaques in arterial walls leading to narrowing and reduced blood flow

Atherosclerosis.risk_groups: smokers, people with high cholesterol, hypertension, diabetes, obesity, sedentary lifestyle, older adults

reduced blood flow or sudden blockage due to plaque rupture

Atherosclerosis.when_to_see_doctor: chest pain, leg pain, risk factors present, routine screening
Atherosclerosis.emergency_signs: sudden chest pain, stroke symptoms, severe limb pain, collapse

Varicose Veins.description: enlarged, twisted veins caused by valve dysfunction leading to poor blood flow, commonly affecting the legs

progression: weakening of vein valves

Varicose Veins.emergency_signs: severe swelling, redness, pain suggesting clot, bleeding
prevention: regular exercise, weight control, avoiding long periods of standing, leg elevation
Varicose Veins.special_notes: common condition, cosmetic and medical concerns, treatments include sclerotherapy and surgery

Pneumonia.description: infection of the lungs causing inflammation of air sacs (alveoli) which may fill with fluid or pus, impairing breathing
Pneumonia.cause: bacteria (e.g., Streptococcus pneumoniae), viruses, fungi, or aspiration of foreign material
Pneumonia.transmission: respiratory droplets, inhalation of infectious agents, aspiration
Pneumonia.risk_groups: infants, elderly, smokers, immunocompromised individuals, people with chronic diseases
progression: infection reaches lungs
inflammation of alveoli
fluid or pus accumulation
impaired oxygen exchange
complications: respiratory failure, sepsis, pleural effusion, lung abscess, death
home_remedy: rest, hydration, fever control, supportive care
avoid: smoking, delayed treatment, exposure to infections
Pneumonia.when_to_see_doctor: high fever, breathing difficulty, chest pain, persistent cough
Pneumonia.emergency_signs: severe breathlessness, bluish lips, confusion, high fever, low oxygen levels
prevention: vaccination (pneumococcal, flu), hand hygiene, avoiding smoking, good nutrition
Pneumonia.contagious_period: varies depending on cause (bacterial or viral)
Pneumonia.special_notes: early treatment improves outcomes, high-risk groups need prompt care, can be life-threatening

Sinusitis.description: inflammation of the sinuses causing blockage and buildup of mucus, often due to infection or allergies
Sinusitis.cause: viral infections (most common), bacterial or fungal infections, allergies, nasal polyps
Sinusitis.transmission: respiratory droplets (in infectious cases), not contagious in non-infectious cases
Sinusitis.risk_groups: people with allergies, asthma, frequent colds, smokers, individuals with weak immune systems
progression: inflammation of sinus lining
blockage of sinus drainage
mucus accumulation
infection or prolonged inflammation
Sinusitis.duration: acute (up to 4 weeks), subacute (4-12 weeks), chronic (more than 12 weeks)
complications: chronic sinusitis, spread of infection to eyes or brain (rare), abscess
home_remedy: steam inhalation, hydration, saline nasal irrigation, rest
avoid: allergens, smoking, untreated infections, poor hygiene
Sinusitis.when_to_see_doctor: symptoms lasting more than 10 days, severe pain, high fever, recurrent infections
Sinusitis.emergency_signs: vision changes, severe headache, swelling around eyes, confusion
prevention: hand hygiene, allergy control, avoiding irritants, vaccination
Sinusitis.contagious_period: varies (only if viral or bacterial cause)
Sinusitis.special_notes: most cases are viral and resolve without antibiotics, chronic cases may require long-term management

Pneumothorax.description: condition where air enters the pleural space causing partial or complete collapse of the lung
Pneumothorax.cause: rupture of lung blebs, chest injury, lung disease (e.g., COPD), medical procedures, spontaneous causes
Pneumothorax.risk_groups: tall thin individuals, smokers, people with lung disease, trauma patients, individuals undergoing chest procedures
symptoms: decreased breath sounds on affected side
progression: air leaks into pleural space
increased pressure compresses lung
partial or complete lung collapse
worsening respiratory distress if untreated
complications: tension pneumothorax, respiratory failure, recurrence
home_remedy: none
avoid: smoking, high-altitude exposure (if prone), untreated lung disease
Pneumothorax.emergency_signs: severe breathlessness, chest tightness, cyanosis, low blood pressure (tension pneumothorax)
prevention: smoking cessation, managing lung diseases, avoiding risk factors
Pneumothorax.special_notes: tension pneumothorax is life-threatening emergency, may require needle decompression or chest tube

Schizophrenia.description: serious mental health condition and psychotic illness that distorts a person's thinking, causing them to lose touch with reality
Schizophrenia.cause: combination of genetics, differences in brain structure and chemicals, pregnancy or birth complications, and trauma
Schizophrenia.risk_groups: starts between ages 16 and 30, men (develop symptoms earlier), people with a family history, individuals who experienced childhood trauma, abuse, or neglect
symptoms: hallucinations (hearing voices or seeing things that are not there)
delusions (unusual false beliefs not based on reality)
muddled thoughts, disorganized speech, and trouble using information
lack of interest in things and difficulty showing emotions
strange movements, psychomotor agitation, or psychomotor retardation
difficulty concentrating, paying attention, or making decisions
feeling fearful, worried, or suspicious that others wish them harm
progression: symptoms may start suddenly or develop slowly over time
positive (psychotic), negative, and cognitive symptoms emerge
episodes of severe symptoms occur, sometimes followed by periods of few or no symptoms
functioning in daily life, keeping a job, and self-care become highly difficult
Schizophrenia.duration: lifelong (though about one third recover completely after one episode)
complications: inability to work or care for oneself, severe relapse, suicidal thoughts
home_remedy: establish a regular routine, get plenty of sleep, eat a healthy diet, exercise regularly
avoid: smoking, recreational drugs, drinking too much alcohol, severe stress
Schizophrenia.when_to_see_doctor: changes in thoughts or behavior that last a long time, current treatments are not helping, warning signs like hearing quiet voices or feeling suspicious appear
Schizophrenia.emergency_signs: mental health crisis, severe psychotic episode, refusing care leading to potential harm
prevention: chance of severe relapse reduced if well-managed, maintain healthy lifestyle and routines
Schizophrenia.special_notes: treated with antipsychotic medication and psychological therapies (CBT, family therapy), advanced statements can be written to record care preferences in case of a serious episode

Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder.description: mental disorder characterized by repeated, unwanted thoughts (obsessions) and irrational, repetitive behaviors (compulsions) performed to reduce anxiety
Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder.cause: unknown, likely a combination of genetics, brain biology and chemistry, and environmental factors
Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder.risk_groups: teens, young adults, boys (develop earlier than girls), people with a first-degree relative with OCD, individuals with childhood trauma
symptoms: repeated unwanted thoughts, urges, or mental images causing anxiety
intense fear of germs, contamination, or losing something
aggressive or forbidden thoughts involving sex or religion
excessive cleaning, handwashing, or ordering things precisely
repeatedly checking things (e.g., locks, ovens) or compulsive counting
sudden twitches, movements, or sounds (if co-occurring with a tic disorder)
progression: intrusive, distressing thought or urge enters the mind (obsession)
obsession causes a feeling of intense anxiety or distress
repetitive behavior or mental act is performed to cope (compulsion)
compulsion brings temporary relief until the anxiety returns and the cycle repeats
complications: depression, eating disorders, generalized anxiety disorder, hoarding disorder, Tourette syndrome, suicidal feelings
home_remedy: utilize self-help guides for mild to moderate symptoms, participate in online or local support groups
avoid: giving in to compulsions without seeking therapy
Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder.when_to_see_doctor: obsessive thoughts and compulsive behaviors affect daily life, unable to manage responsibilities, spending at least 1 hour a day on these thoughts or behaviors
prevention: none
Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder.special_notes: children may develop OCD symptoms following a streptococcal infection (PANDAS), primary treatments include Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (specifically Exposure and Response Prevention) and antidepressants

Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder.description: mental health problem developed after experiencing or witnessing a life-threatening or traumatic event, causing prolonged stress, fear, and flashbacks
Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder.cause: severe trauma such as road accidents, assault, abuse, combat, natural disasters, or the sudden death of a loved one
Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder.risk_groups: women, people with childhood trauma, individuals lacking social support, people with a history of mental illness or substance abuse, emergency service workers, military personnel
Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder.incubation_period: symptoms usually start soon after the event but can appear months or years later
symptoms: nightmares, flashbacks, and intrusive frightening thoughts
physical sensations like pain, sweating, trembling, or feeling sick
feeling alert, on edge, easily startled, or jumpy (hypervigilance)
avoiding people, places, or talking about the trauma
feeling numb, detached from body, or unable to show affection
negative thoughts about self, guilt, blame, or trust issues
anger, irritability, and trouble sleeping or concentrating
progression: person experiences or witnesses a traumatic event
fight-or-flight response triggers intense fear and stress
fear and stress fail to subside naturally over time
re-experiencing, avoidance, arousal, and negative mood symptoms persist and interfere with daily life
Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder.duration: long-term (symptoms must last longer than four weeks for diagnosis, can come and go over years)
complications: depression, substance use, sleep problems, chronic pain
home_remedy: seek support from friends and family, learn coping strategies, join a support group
avoid: using alcohol or drugs to cope, isolating oneself, avoiding thoughts or feelings completely
Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder.when_to_see_doctor: symptoms last longer than 4 weeks after the trauma, symptoms cause great distress or interfere with work and home life
prevention: seek support early, develop coping strategies, learn to respond effectively to fear (resilience factors)
Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder.special_notes: treatments include trauma-focused cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT), Eye Movement Desensitization and Reprocessing (EMDR), and sometimes antidepressants

Panic Disorder.description: type of anxiety disorder causing repeated, sudden periods of intense fear or discomfort (panic attacks) when there is no real danger
Panic Disorder.cause: unknown, likely a combination of genetics, brain biology, environment, and major stress
Panic Disorder.risk_groups: women, late teens or early adults, people under a lot of stress, individuals with a history of childhood trauma
symptoms: sudden, repeated panic attacks of overwhelming anxiety and fear
pounding or racing heart, chest pain
trouble breathing or the feeling of choking
weakness, dizziness, stomach pain, or nausea
feeling out of control or intense fear of death
avoiding places where past attacks occurred
progression: individual experiences a sudden panic attack without warning
physical symptoms like racing heart and shortness of breath peak within minutes
individual develops an intense worry about having another attack
individual begins avoiding places or situations associated with past attacks
Panic Disorder.duration: long-term, individual attacks last a few minutes to over an hour
complications: depression, substance use disorders, agoraphobia
home_remedy: eat regular meals, get enough sleep, exercise regularly, join a support group
avoid: alcohol, caffeine
Panic Disorder.when_to_see_doctor: experiencing repeated panic attacks, anxiety about future attacks interferes with quality of life
Panic Disorder.emergency_signs: severe chest pain or trouble breathing that mimics a heart attack
prevention: healthy lifestyle choices, stress management
Panic Disorder.special_notes: treated with talk therapy (CBT), antidepressants (SSRIs, SNRIs), and anti-anxiety medicines

Osteoarthritis.description: chronic degenerative joint disorder caused by progressive breakdown of cartilage and changes in bone, leading to pain, stiffness, reduced movement, and functional limitation
Osteoarthritis.cause: multifactorial, age-related cartilage degeneration, joint mechanical stress, prior injury, obesity, genetics, abnormal joint structure
Osteoarthritis.risk_groups: older adults, women especially after age 50, overweight or obese individuals, prior joint injury or surgery, repetitive joint overuse, family history, congenital joint abnormalities
symptoms: joint pain worsened by activity, relieved by rest in early stages
stiffness after rest or waking, usually brief morning stiffness
swelling, tenderness, reduced range of motion, weakness around joint
grinding, crunching, crepitus, feeling of bone rubbing
bony enlargements of fingers, enlarged or gnarled joints
difficulty walking, climbing stairs, gripping objects, dressing, standing from chairs
severe persistent pain, joint instability, deformity, disability in advanced disease
progression: cartilage gradually thins and loses cushioning ability
intermittent pain and stiffness develop with use
joint inflammation, swelling, reduced mobility increase
bone spur formation, deformity, chronic pain, disability may occur
Osteoarthritis.common_locations: knees, hips, hands, spine, neck, lower back, feet, thumb base, finger joints
Osteoarthritis.duration: chronic lifelong condition, progresses slowly over years
complications: chronic pain, reduced mobility, falls risk, muscle wasting, depression, sleep disturbance, joint deformity, loss of independence, disability
home_remedy: regular low-impact exercise, weight reduction, heat or cold therapy, joint protection, assistive devices, stretching, rest during flare-ups
avoid: repetitive high-impact joint stress, prolonged inactivity, excessive weight gain, poor posture, unsafe overexertion
Osteoarthritis.when_to_see_doctor: persistent joint pain, swelling, reduced movement, difficulty with daily tasks, worsening symptoms, uncertain diagnosis
Osteoarthritis.emergency_signs: sudden inability to bear weight, hot red swollen joint with fever, severe trauma, sudden weakness or numbness, loss of bladder or bowel control
prevention: maintain healthy weight, regular exercise, strengthen muscles, prevent joint injuries, ergonomic movement habits, manage repetitive strain
Osteoarthritis.special_notes: no cure currently exists, symptoms often improve with lifestyle measures and medicines, joint replacement surgery may help severe cases, differs from autoimmune arthritis because it is primarily degenerative

Rheumatoid Arthritis.description: chronic autoimmune inflammatory disorder that primarily attacks joint linings, causing pain, swelling, stiffness, progressive joint damage, deformity, and possible systemic organ involvement
Rheumatoid Arthritis.cause: autoimmune reaction where the immune system attacks synovium, influenced by genetics, hormones, smoking, environmental triggers
Rheumatoid Arthritis.risk_groups: women, middle-aged adults, smokers, family history, genetically predisposed individuals, people with autoimmune susceptibility
symptoms: symmetrical joint pain, swelling, warmth, tenderness, especially hands, wrists, feet
prolonged morning stiffness, difficulty moving joints, reduced grip strength
redness around joints, decreased range of motion
fatigue, low energy, fever, sweating, poor appetite, weight loss
rheumatoid nodules under skin near pressure points or joints
progressive deformity, weakness, impaired walking or hand use in advanced disease
progression: immune system inflames synovial lining of joints
persistent swelling, pain, stiffness, intermittent flares develop
cartilage, bone, tendons, ligaments become damaged
deformity, disability, extra-articular complications may occur if uncontrolled
Rheumatoid Arthritis.common_locations: hands, wrists, fingers, feet, ankles, knees, elbows, shoulders, neck, other joints
Rheumatoid Arthritis.duration: chronic lifelong condition with relapsing and remitting flares
complications: joint destruction, deformity, carpal tunnel syndrome, lung inflammation, heart inflammation, cardiovascular disease, stroke, osteoporosis, depression, disability
home_remedy: regular gentle exercise, joint protection, balanced rest and activity, heat therapy, stress management, healthy diet, smoking cessation
avoid: smoking, untreated inflammation, prolonged inactivity, excessive joint strain, stopping prescribed medicines without advice
Rheumatoid Arthritis.when_to_see_doctor: persistent joint pain or swelling, morning stiffness over several weeks, reduced function, flare symptoms, medication side effects, unexplained fatigue or weight loss
Rheumatoid Arthritis.emergency_signs: chest pain, severe shortness of breath, sudden neurological symptoms, inability to move joint after rapid swelling, high fever with severe flare, loss of bladder or bowel control
prevention: no guaranteed prevention, avoid smoking, maintain healthy weight, early diagnosis, prompt treatment, regular monitoring
Rheumatoid Arthritis.special_notes: early treatment with DMARDs or biologics can slow damage significantly, symptoms often fluctuate with flares and remissions, pregnancy planning is important because some medicines are unsafe in pregnancy

Low Back Pain.description: common symptom involving pain or discomfort in the lower back, usually mechanical and self-limiting, but occasionally caused by nerve compression, injury, infection, cancer, or serious spinal disorders
Low Back Pain.cause: muscle strain, ligament sprain, disc degeneration, herniated disc, poor movement patterns, prolonged sitting, awkward lifting, overuse, arthritis, spinal stenosis, trauma, less commonly infection or tumor
Low Back Pain.risk_groups: adults of all ages, sedentary individuals, heavy manual workers, obesity, poor conditioning, older adults, prior back problems, repetitive lifting occupations
symptoms: aching, stiffness, soreness, muscle spasm in lower back
sharp, burning, stabbing, shooting pain in back or buttock
pain radiating into one or both legs, sciatica
pins and needles, numbness, weakness from nerve irritation
pain worse with bending, lifting, prolonged sitting, certain movements
reduced mobility, difficulty standing upright, trouble walking or getting out of bed
severe constant night pain, unexplained weight loss, fever, bladder or bowel changes may indicate serious cause
progression: sudden or gradual onset of lumbar pain occurs
stiffness and movement limitation develop during acute phase
most mechanical cases improve within days to weeks with activity and self-care
some cases become chronic, recurrent, or reveal underlying structural disease
Low Back Pain.common_locations: lower back, lumbar spine, buttocks, hips, back of thigh, legs, feet when nerve-related
Low Back Pain.duration: acute days to 6 weeks, subacute 6-12 weeks, chronic over 12 weeks
complications: chronic pain, reduced mobility, work disability, depression, sleep disturbance, falls risk, persistent sciatica, cauda equina syndrome, neurological deficits
home_remedy: stay active, gentle walking, gradual exercises, heat or ice packs, posture changes, short-term pain relief medicines if appropriate, avoid prolonged bed rest
avoid: prolonged inactivity, excessive bed rest, awkward heavy lifting, repeated painful twisting, fear-based immobilization, unnecessary early imaging without warning signs
Low Back Pain.when_to_see_doctor: pain lasting over 6 weeks, worsening pain, leg weakness, numbness, night pain, pain not affected by movement, history of cancer, fever, significant trauma
Low Back Pain.emergency_signs: loss of bladder or bowel control, urinary retention, saddle numbness, rapidly worsening leg weakness, inability to walk, severe trauma, fever with severe back pain
prevention: regular exercise, core and back strengthening, healthy weight, ergonomic lifting, frequent movement breaks, maintain flexibility, stop smoking
Low Back Pain.special_notes: most cases do not need early X-ray or MRI, imaging is usually reserved for red flags or persistent symptoms, MRI may show age-related changes that are not the true pain source

Fibromyalgia.description: chronic pain syndrome characterized by widespread musculoskeletal pain, heightened pain sensitivity, fatigue, sleep disturbance, and cognitive symptoms without ongoing tissue damage
Fibromyalgia.cause: exact cause unknown, abnormal central pain processing, nervous system sensitization, genetic predisposition, stress-related and environmental triggers
Fibromyalgia.risk_groups: women, adults aged 35-60, family history, people with anxiety or depression, chronic stress exposure, obesity, rheumatoid arthritis, lupus, trauma history
symptoms: widespread body pain described as aching, burning, stabbing, or mixed pain
increased sensitivity to touch, light, temperature, noise, odors, or medicines
tender points in neck, shoulders, elbows, hips, knees, back of head
fatigue despite adequate sleep, low energy, poor stamina
muscle stiffness, spasms, pain that moves around body
numbness, tingling, pins and needles in hands or feet
memory or concentration problems, fibro fog
dizziness, balance issues, irritable bowel syndrome, restless legs syndrome
progression: widespread pain and fatigue gradually or suddenly begin
symptoms fluctuate with stress, weather, activity, sleep quality, illness
recurrent flares and remissions occur over time
chronic symptoms may persist but can improve with management
Fibromyalgia.common_locations: widespread muscles and soft tissues, neck, shoulders, back, hips, knees, elbows, head, jaw
Fibromyalgia.duration: chronic long-term condition, often months to years
complications: reduced quality of life, sleep disorders, depression, anxiety, reduced work capacity, deconditioning, chronic fatigue, cognitive impairment
home_remedy: regular gentle exercise, pacing activities, sleep hygiene, stress reduction, relaxation techniques, heat therapy, balanced routine, self-management strategies
avoid: overexertion, prolonged inactivity, unmanaged stress, irregular sleep patterns, expecting complete bed rest to help, abrupt activity spikes
Fibromyalgia.when_to_see_doctor: widespread pain over 3 months, persistent fatigue, poor sleep, memory issues, symptoms affecting daily life, uncertain diagnosis
Fibromyalgia.emergency_signs: severe suicidal thoughts, chest pain, sudden neurological deficits, high fever, rapidly worsening unexplained symptoms suggesting another condition
prevention: no proven prevention, regular exercise, stress management, healthy sleep habits, healthy weight, early treatment of associated mood disorders
Fibromyalgia.special_notes: fibromyalgia does not damage muscles or organs and is not life-threatening, diagnosis is clinical after excluding other causes, pain medicines alone are often less effective than combined lifestyle and multidisciplinary treatment

Tendinitis.description: painful inflammatory or degenerative condition affecting tendons around joints, commonly caused by overuse, injury, or repetitive motion
Tendinitis.cause: repetitive strain, sudden injury, overuse, poor biomechanics, sports activity, occupational stress, aging changes
Tendinitis.risk_groups: athletes, manual workers, repetitive motion workers, older adults, people with poor posture, prior joint injury
symptoms: localized pain near a joint or tendon
pain worsened by movement or resistance
swelling, stiffness, reduced range of motion
weakness or difficulty using affected limb
sudden severe pain or popping may suggest tendon rupture
progression: overuse or injury irritates tendon
inflammation and pain develop with activity
persistent irritation causes weakness, stiffness, recurring pain
chronic degeneration or rupture may occur if untreated
Tendinitis.common_locations: shoulder, wrist, elbow, neck, hip, knee, ankle, heel, Achilles tendon
Tendinitis.duration: acute days to weeks, chronic cases may last months
complications: chronic pain, reduced mobility, tendon rupture, recurrent inflammation, joint stiffness, weakness, work limitation
home_remedy: rest, ice, compression, elevation, temporary activity reduction, gentle stretching after acute pain improves, ergonomic changes
avoid: repetitive painful motions, returning to activity too quickly, ignoring worsening symptoms
Tendinitis.when_to_see_doctor: pain lasting more than a few weeks, recurrent swelling, reduced movement, weakness, suspected infection, uncertain diagnosis
Tendinitis.emergency_signs: fever with red hot swollen joint, inability to move limb, sudden tendon snap, severe swelling, rapidly worsening pain
prevention: warm up before exercise, stretch regularly, use proper technique, take rest breaks, vary repetitive tasks, strengthen supporting muscles, maintain healthy weight
Tendinitis.special_notes: imaging such as X-ray, ultrasound, or MRI is often unnecessary initially unless symptoms persist or recur, corticosteroid injections may provide short-term relief, surgery is uncommon except ruptures or resistant cases

Bursitis.description: painful inflammation of a bursa, a small fluid-filled sac that cushions bones, tendons, muscles, or skin near joints, commonly caused by overuse or pressure
Bursitis.cause: repetitive motion, prolonged pressure on joints, kneeling, leaning on elbows, acute injury, friction, infection, gout, inflammatory arthritis
Bursitis.risk_groups: athletes, manual workers, people who kneel often, people leaning on elbows, older adults, people with gout, rheumatoid arthritis, diabetes, prior joint injury
symptoms: pain worsened by movement or pressure
pain while resting on affected side or surface
fever or marked redness may suggest infection
progression: repeated stress or injury irritates the bursa
fluid accumulation and inflammation develop
pain and swelling limit joint use
chronic thickening, recurrence, or infection may occur if untreated
Bursitis.common_locations: knee, elbow, shoulder, hip, heel, ankle
Bursitis.duration: acute days to weeks, chronic or recurrent cases may last months
complications: chronic pain, reduced mobility, recurrent bursitis, infection, surrounding tendon irritation, functional limitation
home_remedy: rest, ice, avoid pressure on joint, compression if appropriate, elevation, gradual return to activity, padding of affected area
avoid: kneeling on hard surfaces, leaning on elbows, repetitive painful movements, continuing aggravating activity
Bursitis.when_to_see_doctor: persistent swelling, severe pain, recurrent episodes, reduced movement, suspected infection, symptoms not improving with rest
Bursitis.emergency_signs: fever, rapidly increasing redness, severe swelling, inability to move joint, severe pain, spreading infection signs
prevention: use knee or elbow pads, take movement breaks, proper technique during activity, avoid prolonged pressure, strengthen supporting muscles, manage gout or arthritis
Bursitis.special_notes: diagnosis is often clinical, fluid aspiration may be used to rule out infection or crystals, steroid injection or surgery may be considered for persistent cases

Carpal Tunnel Syndrome.description: common nerve compression disorder caused by pressure on the median nerve within the wrist carpal tunnel, leading to pain, numbness, tingling, weakness, and reduced hand function
Carpal Tunnel Syndrome.cause: compression of the median nerve in the carpal tunnel due to swelling of tendons, inflammation, repetitive strain, wrist anatomy changes, pregnancy, hormonal changes, or associated medical conditions
Carpal Tunnel Syndrome.risk_groups: women, middle-aged or older adults, pregnancy, overweight individuals, repetitive hand workers, diabetes, rheumatoid arthritis, hypothyroidism, menopause, prior wrist fracture
symptoms: numbness, tingling, burning in thumb, index, middle, and part of ring finger
wrist or hand pain, often worse at night or early morning
weakness, clumsiness, dropping objects, reduced grip strength
difficulty with buttoning clothes, holding phone, book, or steering wheel
shaking hand for relief, sensation of swelling without visible swelling
severe cases may show thumb muscle wasting and persistent numbness
progression: intermittent numbness or tingling develops, especially at night
symptoms increase with gripping, bending wrist, or repetitive hand use
persistent pain, sensory loss, and hand weakness occur
untreated severe cases may cause muscle wasting and functional impairment
Carpal Tunnel Syndrome.common_locations: wrist carpal tunnel, palm side of hand, thumb, index finger, middle finger, radial half of ring finger
Carpal Tunnel Syndrome.duration: variable, weeks to years depending on cause and treatment
complications: chronic pain, persistent numbness, grip weakness, thenar muscle wasting, reduced dexterity, permanent nerve damage if prolonged
home_remedy: nighttime wrist splinting, activity modification, ergonomic changes, rest breaks, wrist positioning neutral, gentle hand exercises
avoid: prolonged wrist bending, repetitive squeezing or gripping, delaying treatment when weakness develops, constant splint use without guidance
Carpal Tunnel Syndrome.when_to_see_doctor: symptoms lasting more than several weeks, worsening numbness, weakness, dropping objects, sleep disruption, reduced hand function, uncertain diagnosis
Carpal Tunnel Syndrome.emergency_signs: sudden severe hand weakness, rapidly worsening numbness, loss of hand function, signs of trauma with deformity, severe swelling or infection
prevention: ergonomic workplace setup, regular breaks from repetitive tasks, neutral wrist posture, weight management, diabetes control, treatment of thyroid or inflammatory disease
Carpal Tunnel Syndrome.special_notes: diagnosis is mainly clinical and may use Phalen test, Tinel sign, nerve conduction studies, ultrasound, or MRI, pregnancy-related cases often improve after delivery, surgery may be needed when conservative treatment fails
